_comment: Actions that reach OUT to infrastructure that is not ours, in a way that is attributable and cannot be undone. hooks/actionguard.py turns each match into a confirmation prompt with the briefing below. RULE 1: capability names and flags only — never a case target. Tuning: adding an entry costs one prompt; removing one silently removes a safety rail, so prefer narrowing `flag_required` over deleting a row. An entry with `flag_required` only fires when that flag is present, which is how a tool whose DEFAULT path really is safe (capture_evidence archives only when asked) stays unprompted for ordinary use. `flag_required` is NOT enough when the default path is itself outbound: the MCP surface is typed, so CLI flag text never reaches tool_input and the row would read as coverage while allowing every call. Use `outbound_by_default` there — it names the opt-outs (`unless_env`, `unless_params`) instead of the flag, and gates on what the call actually does.

mcp_tools._comment: Matched against the PreToolUse tool_name for MCP tools, i.e. mcp__<server>__<tool>. The server segment is ignored so a differently-named registration is still covered.

engage_account.why: Creates an account on the TARGET's platform and logs in. The operator sees a new registration, its timing, and whatever egress path it came from. It cannot be un-registered.
engage_account.before: Confirm the persona is synthetic, that egress is not your own address, and that you are authorized to interact with this target.

harvest_authenticated.why: Drives an authenticated session inside the target's members area — every page it touches is a logged request tied to the account you created.
harvest_authenticated.before: Only run this on a session you deliberately opened. Each fetch adds to the operator's picture of the account.

anyrun_submit.why: Detonates a sample in a PUBLIC sandbox. Operators watch for their own samples; the standard response is to rotate the backend, revoke the signing key and re-skin the front — destroying the infrastructure the case rests on.
anyrun_submit.before: A public task is world-readable and irreversible. Detonation is the analyst's decision on a private plan, never a side effect of a pivot.

capture_evidence.why: With --submit this asks a third-party archive to fetch the target, which tells that archive — and anyone reading it — that the URL is under investigation.
capture_evidence.before: Archiving is usually right for evidence. Confirm you want the request attributed now rather than after collection.

pivot_extract.why: Collection is NOT passive by default: the harness appends --submit, asking Wayback Save-Page-Now and urlscan to fetch the target. Wayback keeps a permanent PUBLIC snapshot showing the URL was under investigation, and when. urlscan defaults to unlisted.
pivot_extract.before: Archiving is right for evidence and wrong for a target you have not decided to touch. Set HARNESS_NO_ARCHIVE=1 (or pass no_archive) to collect without submitting.

outbound_by_default.note: Gated on BEHAVIOUR, not flag text: the typed MCP surface never carries --submit (collect_core.py appends it inside the harness subprocess), so flag_required alone can never fire here. It still covers the shell front-end and the archiving-disabled case.

misp_push.why: Writes the event to your MISP instance. Staged organisation-only and unpublished, so it stays inside your org and an unpublished event can still be deleted — but it is a real write to a shared system your colleagues read, and it leaves an audit trail under your API key.
misp_push.before: Check the TLP and distribution are what you intend BEFORE the write, not after. Correcting them later means editing an event other people may already have opened.

misp_publish.why: PUBLISHES the event so it syncs to the community. This is the irreversible one: a MISP event pushed to peers cannot be recalled, and every indicator in it becomes somebody else's blocking rule. A false positive here blocks innocent infrastructure on networks you will never see.
misp_publish.before: Confirm every attribute survives false-positive control (run /cti-check on the clustering indicators), that the TLP matches what the source permits, and that the analyst has explicitly asked to disseminate. Staging with push first is the reversible option.

bash_patterns._comment: Substrings matched against a Bash tool_input.command. The engine is reachable from the shell as well as over MCP, and a gate that only covers one of the two front-ends is not a gate.

entries.why: Engage: registers/logs in on the target (outbound, attributable, irreversible).
Engage: drives the authenticated session inside the target's members area.

Engage via the T2 dispatcher — registers/logs in on the target. The trailing space is load-bearing: it keeps `intel.py engage-report`, which only renders a local write-up, from prompting. Over-prompting is how a safety rail gets switched off.
Engage via the T2 dispatcher — drives the authenticated session.
ANY.RUN: this is the flag that actually detonates the sample in the public sandbox.
Asks a third-party archive/scanner to fetch the target, publishing the URL and the timing.
IntelShare: writes the event to your MISP instance (staged, organisation-only).
IntelShare: PUBLISHES to the community — irreversible; the event cannot be recalled and its indicators become other people's blocking rules.
IntelShare via the T2 dispatcher — writes the event to your MISP instance.
IntelShare via the T2 dispatcher — PUBLISHES to the community; irreversible.
